exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.explanation:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}1} \\ -3& 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{31}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{32}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{33}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{34}} \\ &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+1} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+4}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1\\ 0 & -4 & -2\\ -3& 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= 2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} - \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1\\ 0 & -4 & -2\\ -3& 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, computing the first $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0} \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{31}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{32}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{33}} \\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+1}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+2} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1\\ -4 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - 2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1\\ -4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (1-2) - 2(2-4) \\[5pt] &= -1 + 4 \\[5pt] &= 3 \end{align*}

Now, computing the second $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1\\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}-4} & {\color{red}-2} \\ -3& 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{21}} +{\color{red}(-4)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{22}} +{\color{red}(-2)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{23}} \\ &= {\color{red}(-4)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}(-2)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2\\ -3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= -4 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} +2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2\\ -3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= -4(2+3) + 2 (1+6) \\[5pt] &= -20 + 14 \\[5pt] &= -6 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3& 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 2 \cdot 3 - (-6) = 12. \]

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.text: Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd row: \[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| \]
question.explanation:
Using cofactor expansion along the third row, we have \begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{31}} + {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{32}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{33}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{34}} \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+2} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| }\\[5pt] &= -2 \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| \\ \end{align*}

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{ccc} {\color{red}4} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{11}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{12}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{13}}\\ &= {\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+1} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{cc} 3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= 4 \left| \begin{array}{cc} 3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| \\[5pt] &= 4 (3\cdot 2 - (-1) \cdot (-2)) \\[5pt] &= 4 \cdot 4\\[5pt] &= 16 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{array} \right| = -2\cdot 16 = -32. \]

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.text:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row:
\[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right|. \]
question.explanation:
Using cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{red}4} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0}& {\color{red}0} \\ \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{41}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{42}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{43}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{44}} \\ &= {\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{4+1} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= -4\left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 3 & 1 \\ {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{21}} + {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{22}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{23}} \\ &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+1} \cdot \left| \begin{array}{cc} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{array} \right|} \\[5pt] &= -2\left| \begin{array}{cc} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{array} \right| \\[5pt] &= -2(9-2)\\[3pt] &= -14 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right| = -4 \cdot (-14) = 56. \]

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.explanation:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ -2& 1 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{31}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{32}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{33}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{34}} \\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+1} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2\\ 0 & 2 & -1\\ -2& 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix} -2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2\\ 0 & 2 & -1\\ -2& 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, computing the first $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}5} \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{31}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{32}} +{\color{red}5} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{33}} \\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+1}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}5} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{3+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1\\ -3 & 2 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} + 5 \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1\\ -3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (1-4) + 5(6-3) \\[5pt] &= -3 + 15 \\[5pt] &= 12 \end{align*}

Now, computing the second $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2\\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-1}\\ -2& 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{21}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{22}} +{\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{23}} \\ &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1\\ -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= 2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1\\ -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2(5+4) + (0-2) \\[5pt] &= 18 - 2 \\[5pt] &= 16 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2& 1 & 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \cdot 12 - 2 \cdot 16= -20. \]

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

question.explanation:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}-1} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}1} \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2& 0 & -3 & 3 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{21}} +{\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{22}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{23}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{24}} \\ &= {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+2} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+4}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2\\ 2 & 3 & 1\\ 2& 0 & -3 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= - \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2\\ 2 & 3 & 1\\ 2& 0 & -3 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, computing the first $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-1}\\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{11}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{12}} +{\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{13}} \\ &= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}(-1)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 2 & -3 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &=-2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} - \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 2 & -3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= -2(6-2) - (-6-2) \\[5pt] &= -8 - (-8) \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

Finally, we compute the second $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}2} \\ 2 & 3 & 1\\ 2& 0 & -3 \end{vmatrix} &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{11}} +{\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{12}} +{\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{13}} \\ &= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{vmatrix}} + {\color{red}(2)} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{1+3} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3\\ 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix}} \\[5pt] &= -\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{vmatrix} +2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3\\ 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= -(-6-2) + 2 (0-6) \\[5pt] &= -(-8) + 2\cdot(-6) \\[5pt] &= 8-12\\[5pt] &=-4 \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3& 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -0 + (-4) = -4. \]

question.explanation:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

\begin{align*} \left| \begin{array}{cccc} 3 & -1 & 4& {\color{red}0} \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & {\color{red}5} \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & {\color{red}0} \\ 1 & 2 & 4 & {\color{red}0} \end{array} \right| &= {\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{14}} +{\color{red}5} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{24}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{black}C_{34}} +{\color{red}0} \cdot {\color{blue}C_{44}} \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}5} \cdot {\color{blue}(-1)^{2+4}\cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{array} \right| } \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \end{array} \right|. \end{align*}
